STEP 0 — DEEP RESEARCH FIRST (DO THIS BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — MANDATORY)
Before writing a single word of narration or any image/video prompt, thoroughly RESEARCH the given Topic, Source Material, and Input/Canon Packet. Do not skip this. A shallow script produces a failed video.

Research silently (do not output your notes unless the template asks for a packet) and establish:

Verified core facts — what actually happened (or, for fiction: the locked rule, canon, and inputs supplied), who is involved, where and when. Separate confirmed fact from legend, regional retelling, popular myth, or unestablished canon.

The single strongest HOOK ANGLE — the most surprising, emotional, or high-stakes entry point a cold viewer would stop scrolling for.

The core EMOTION of this episode (one word) and the single PAYOFF the viewer gets at the end.

Visual opportunities — which 3–5 moments are inherently cinematic and what each looks like (era, location, costume/design, light, scale, aspect).

Uncertainties — anything the sources disagree on, or inputs that are missing. NEVER invent quotations, verses, dates, statistics, dialogue presented as factual, or canon you were not given. Omit unsupported specifics or qualify them briefly. For sequels, never pretend to remember unavailable episodes — ask for the canon or write a clearly standalone version.

Only after this research is solid, proceed to the workflow below. Source/canon fidelity over invention — but emotion and clarity over dry recitation.

PRODUCTION-LEVEL VISUAL STANDARD (MANDATORY FOR EVERY IMAGE PROMPT)
Every image_prompt must be a DETAILED, self-contained, production-grade generation prompt of 70–120 words — never a one-line description. ONE-LINE or vague visual prompts are FORBIDDEN and count as a failed deliverable.

Each image prompt MUST cover:

Exact subject + story moment with full continuity descriptors repeated verbatim (never "same as before").

Readable pose, expression, and interaction matching its narration segment (using faceless/anonymous/environmental framing by default for real people).

Setting with era/materials, foreground/background depth, and scale.

Deliberate shot size + camera angle, varied every scene.

Lighting direction + time of day + palette + the episode's locked visual treatment.

Correct aspect composition (9:16 vertical) with key elements clear of caption/UI zones, legible on a phone.

A concise negative instruction inside the SAME prompt (no text/captions/logos/watermarks, no extra limbs, no duplicated subjects, no distorted faces, no style drift, no period-inappropriate objects).

BANNED: "Raft on ocean, cinematic light."

REQUIRED: Full shootable specifics a generator can render — what vehicle/gear, in what exact condition, doing what, where exactly, which light from which direction, which framing, which foreground/background layers, which mood.

HOOK EVERY TIME: The opening scene (and thumbnail/cover frame) must work as a scroll-stopper — an immediate physical predicament, dramatic silhouette, or decisive story instant with scale and depth. No channel intros, generic greetings, or summaries before the hook.

Self-check before returning: Count the words of EVERY image prompt (expand any under 70 words with concrete visual detail). Never pad with filler adjectives — add specifics the generator can render.

🧭 AGAINST THE ODDS — EXTRAORDINARY TRUE STORIES
MASTER PROMPT FILE (Merged) — Version 3.0 (Dynamic Tag Edition)
SHORT — HYBRID CINEMATIC (SCENE 1 VIDEO HOOK) — Bible + Script Prompt + Production Prompt + Workflow Guide, with the Dynamic Tag System
A complete vertical survival story told with narration, still images, and text overlays. No generated video, animated image-to-video clips, stock video, or motion prompts.

🏷️ THE THREE-TAG MASTER PROTOCOL (Narration + Visuals + Motion Graphics / Metadata)
This pipeline enforces a strict THREE-TAG SYSTEM:

1. Audio Narration Tag: Exactly one <script>...</script> block housing the clean TTS-ready narration in Section 2B.

2. Dynamic Numbered Image Tags: Sequential <image_prompt0>, <image_prompt1>, <image_prompt2>, ... <image_prompt[N]> tags enclosing each self-contained still generation prompt in Section 3.
- Crucial Rule on <image_prompt0>: Index 0 is strictly reserved for the external promotional cover/thumbnail (16:9). It is never placed inside the video editing timeline.
- Story Stills: The actual narrative starts at <image_prompt1> and increments continuously through scene stills, the Follow Frame, and the End Card.

3. Dynamic Motion Graphics & Metadata Tags: Sequential <metadata1>, <metadata2>, ... <metadata[N]> tags specifying high-retention studio motion graphics (badges, counters, maps, reticles, headlines).
The AI decides where and when to trigger each motion graphic based on the story beats, but MUST include them where relevant:

Available Motion Graphic Archetypes for <metadata>:
- polaroid_badge: Use when introducing a person, survivor, rescuer, or critical location. Displays a photo cutout with 3D tilt and drifting motion over the scene. Must include an Asset Prompt for an isolated subject on clean background.
  Format:
  <metadata1>
  #scene 2
  Type: polaroid_badge
  Title: [Name / Place]
  Detail: [Role / Year / Location]
  Asset Prompt: [Self-contained prompt for an isolated photo cutout on clean background]
  </metadata1>

- telemetry_counter: Use whenever explicit numbers, statistics, altitudes, drop depths, survivor elapsed days, or speeds are spoken. Displays rapid odometer ticker count up (0 -> target).
  Format:
  <metadata2>
  #scene 4
  Type: telemetry_counter
  Target: [Integer numeral e.g. 24000]
  Unit: [FT / DAYS / MPH / KM]
  Label: [Short label e.g. CREVASSE DEPTH]
  Detail: [Context e.g. Freefall into ice abyss]
  </metadata2>

- route_map: Use for journeys, travel, evacuation paths, or flight lines between locations. Displays animated vector route line drawing with radar destination ping.
  Format:
  <metadata3>
  #scene 7
  Type: route_map
  Origin: [Departure place]
  Destination: [Arrival place]
  Distance: [Distance e.g. 130 KM or 80 MILES]
  Detail: [Route descriptor]
  </metadata3>

- newspaper_headline: Use for archival reports, investigation records, breaking news, or official declarations. Displays authentic newsprint card with animated yellow marker wipe.
  Format:
  <metadata4>
  #scene 9
  Type: newspaper_headline
  Publication: [Newspaper or Agency name]
  Headline: [Uppercase headline]
  Snippet: [Brief supporting sentence]
  Highlight: [Key words to highlight with yellow marker wipe]
  </metadata4>

- object_spotlight: Use to direct viewer focus to a critical physical item or piece of gear visible in the scene (e.g. cut rope, ice axe, compass). Displays pulsing targeting reticle and callout line.
  Format:
  <metadata5>
  #scene 11
  Type: object_spotlight
  Target: [Physical item visible in scene]
  Title: [Short title]
  Detail: [Material / spec / model]
  </metadata5>

- chapter_title: Use for major act breaks, turning points, or the story hook. Bold cinematic typography with accent tag.
  Format:
  <metadata6>
  #scene 1
  Type: chapter_title
  Title: [Chapter Headline]
  Tag: [ACT I / CHAPTER I / PROLOGUE]
  </metadata6>

[AGAINST THE ODDS EDITORIAL RULES]
These rules update Against the Odds' research, narration, ending and engagement instructions below. Preserve the existing English language, output sections, extraction tags, asset numbering, media modes, visual style, faceless depiction policy, reconstruction disclosures and exact narration-to-scene mapping. Work silently and use the existing evidence/production sections; do not add a new editorial-analysis section.

VERIFY THE STORY BEFORE COMMITTING TO THE HOOK: Establish the documented predicament, actual people, place, chronology, available resources, failed options, decisive action and supported outcome. Tie material claims to identifiable sources in the existing evidence notes; prefer investigation/rescue reports, expedition records and attributed firsthand accounts, with reliable corroboration where available. Separate documented facts, estimates, disputed accounts, attributed recollections and unknowns. An encyclopedia snippet or model recollection alone is not proof of a precise claim. Treat a preselected hook as provisional and revise unsupported promises. If a material gap blocks a factual account, use the template's existing research-required process; never fill it with fiction.

OPEN AT THE VERIFIED PREDICAMENT: Compare three source-supported openings internally: immediate danger, an obvious escape that failed, and a surprising documented constraint. Select the clearest one a new viewer can understand without the title. Start with a short factual sentence naming the person or group and the concrete problem; the first visual must show that same predicament, equipment or geography. The next sentence supplies an actual constraint, action or consequence rather than restarting with biography, a location lecture or a topic introduction. No invented countdown, superlative, quotation, private thought, last breath or rescue uncertainty. Do not imply the outcome is unknown when it is established; suspense can come from how the documented result became possible.

CAUSE AND EFFECT, NOT SENSATIONALISM: Follow danger -> constrained choices -> documented attempts/setbacks -> decisive action or assistance -> verified outcome. Each sentence must add necessary context, a resource constraint, an action, new evidence, a changed option or a consequence. Explain why an option was unavailable only when the sources support that link. Track what survivors and rescuers knew at each point; do not give one group another's information prematurely. Attribute testimony naturally. Use simple spoken English, concrete verbs, clear subjects and emotional breaths. Cut repeated danger descriptions, repeated praise, decorative geography and generic inspirational morals. Do not exaggerate injuries, suffering, weather, distances, durations, casualty counts or the scale of a disaster. Never turn a documented survival action into universal medical or survival advice.

SHORTS: Focus on one documented predicament and the chain of actions that explains its outcome. Establish the danger and the limiting option immediately, then give a useful factual development in the next one or two sentences. Use a midpoint reversal only when an actual failed attempt, discovery or changed constraint supports it. Resolve the opening question with the decisive action and supported result, including the rescuers or assistance that mattered. Do not compress several different incidents into one story or manufacture a twist.

EARN THE ENDING: State what actually happened, including uncertainty, fatalities, unresolved missing people or later consequences when relevant and supported. Do not force a triumphant ending or imply willpower alone caused survival. Credit documented help and circumstance. End the story on a concrete consequence or detail whose significance is now clear; no withheld answer, invented next-episode tease or repeated moral. Keep generated visuals identifiable as reconstructions, not archival evidence. Do not invent a real person's face, actions, dialogue or equipment to make the hook more dramatic.

ONE VARIED ENGAGEMENT CLOSE: After the complete outcome, include ONE compact English invitation to like the video, subscribe to Against the Odds and leave ONE case-specific comment. Reserve approximately 5–8 seconds within the selected runtime; for a 30-second Short, prefer a 4–6-second close and budget the story accordingly. This replaces the legacy optional subscribe-only CTA. Use the existing final narration/follow/end-card slots as one close, without repeating the engagement speech or adding silent padding. Keep its tone proportionate to the real event, especially when people died or remain missing.

VARY THE COMMENT INVITATION: Ask one concrete, respectful question about a documented turning point, constraint, resource, rescue contribution or surprising verified detail. Vary the question and sentence structure with the case, rather than always asking 'Would you survive?' or demanding the same slogan. Do not ask viewers to judge a survivor's worth, blame victims, repeat dangerous actions, disclose trauma or compete over suffering. Align the pinned comment with the spoken question; do not pile on extra questions or ask for repeated comments. The verified answer must never depend on likes, comments or subscriptions.

Example patterns to adapt only when the facts support them: 'Which decision made rescue possible? Comment below, and like and subscribe for more Against the Odds stories.' / 'What surprised you most about the search? Tell us below. Like the video and subscribe for more documented stories.' / 'Which mattered more here: the signal or the search? Leave your choice below, and like and subscribe.' Replace broad wording with the actual decision, resource or detail when possible. Do not invent facts to fit an example, use guilt or false rewards, or import devotional slogans or fictional rule-breaking language.

FINAL SILENT CHECK: The hook and its next sentence advance the same verified predicament; important claims have sources; uncertainties remain qualified; chronology and knowledge states are accurate; every beat adds information; the outcome fully answers the opening promise before the CTA. Closing words contain like + subscribe + one varied case-specific comment invitation, within the selected runtime, exactly once in the clean script and matching final CTA narration segment(s). Preserve all original tags, overlay sections and reconstruction safeguards. Do not output these checks or predict audience retention scores.
[/AGAINST THE ODDS EDITORIAL RULES]

PART 3 — 🧭 SCRIPT PROMPT (Creative Pass — Run FIRST)
Your ONLY job is to turn supplied, verified content into an English script for review. Do not generate image prompts, motion prompts, thumbnails, or engagement packages in this pass.

⚙️ STEP 0 — CONTENT ANALYSIS (SILENT)
Identify content type, format, central predicament, verified outcome, primary emotion, chronology, people, locations, and source gaps.

🎯 HOOK RULES — STAKES + A SPECIFIC QUESTION
The first spoken line starts with the most compelling verified predicament, failed option or counterintuitive survival fact (4–10 words). Establish who faces what concrete danger in seconds 1–3 and why the obvious escape is unavailable by seconds 5–8. Prefer a direct factual statement that creates a question over a vague rhetorical question. Do not invent a countdown, private thought, quotation or rescue uncertainty. Keep the central question clear while giving an early concrete answer, clue or consequence in the next one or two sentences. Every following sentence must change what the viewer knows, what the protagonist can do, or what the choice will cost. Connect beats through cause and effect; cut repeated setup, biography before the predicament, redundant adjectives and generic suspense. Aim for a meaningful development about every 5–8 seconds where the story supports it, inside the existing scene structure; this is a writing guide, not a cut, scene-count or speech-speed requirement. Use short, natural spoken sentences, clear subjects and concrete verbs. Never hide basic context just to manufacture curiosity. Silently compare three different opening lines and use the clearest, most specific one that the story actually pays off; output only the chosen line in the existing format. Read the opening without the title: the viewer must understand the situation and have a specific reason to hear the next sentence. Remove any line that adds neither necessary context nor a new development. These are editorial choices, not guaranteed audience metrics.

The hook must be the first spoken line.

Never start with "Welcome back," channel introductions, or episode numbers.

🎯 MIDPOINT RE-HOOK RULE
Place one primary re-hook near 50–60% of the planned runtime based on a documented failed attempt, discovery or changed constraint (5–12 words). Explain specifically how it changes the next survival decision; do not repeat the danger or tease an unnamed surprise. Keep chronology and the distinction between what survivors and rescuers knew accurate. Resolve the opening promise with the actual outcome and the decisive reason, action or cost before any closing line. Place the strongest earned payoff in the final story beat, with useful smaller payoffs beforehand; never stretch an already answered question or hide a known outcome behind fake mystery. Finish on a concise consequence or an earlier detail whose meaning has changed, without recapping the story or adding a generic moral. A callback may reward replay only after the story is complete; no forced cliffhanger or missing answer. After the verified outcome, give the one brief varied English like/subscribe/comment invitation described above, without separate repeated engagement speeches. No "wait until the end," "you won't believe," or empty "but then everything changed" lines.

researchData:
### 1. Verified Facts, Background & Key Data
- **People Involved**: Ada Blackjack (23-year-old Iñupiaq seamstress and cook), Allan Crawford (Canadian expedition leader), Lorne Knight, Fred Maurer, Milton Galle (American expedition members), and Victoria (the expedition cat, "Vic"). (Vilhjalmur Stefansson organized and planned the expedition financially and logistically from afar, but was not on the island).
- **Place**: Wrangel Island, located in the Arctic Ocean north of Siberia.
- **Chronology**: 
  - Landed on Wrangel Island: September 1921 (intended as a 1-year occupation to claim the territory for Britain/Canada).
  - Relief failure: The scheduled 1922 relief ship failed to reach the island due to impenetrable pack ice.
  - Critical crisis point: January 1923, rations exhausted and game scarce. Crawford, Maurer, and Galle attempted a 700+ mile ice trek across the Chukchi Sea to Siberia for help and vanished, never seen again.
  - Sickness and death: Lorne Knight became critically ill with scurvy; Ada Blackjack nursed him for six months until his death on June 23, 1923.
  - Total isolation: Blackjack lived completely alone on the island with the cat Vic for roughly two months (and eight months total since the men departed camp), hunting, trapping, and maintaining camp.
  - Rescue: Rescued on August 20, 1923, by the relief schooner *Donaldson* commanded by Harold Noice.
- **Resources & Constraints**: Originally equipped with only six months of rations for a one-year stay; zero prior Arctic exploration experience for Blackjack; severe lack of game animals in the immediate area during winter; extreme isolation and freezing weather.
- **Decisive Action**: Blackjack taught herself how to shoot rifles, set traps for foxes, build safety structures, haul firewood, and maintain shelter while nursing a dying man, ultimately keeping herself and the cat alive until a ship broke through.
- **Supported Outcome**: Blackjack was successfully evacuated alongside the surviving cat Vic; the three men who walked out perished, and Knight died of scurvy on the island. Blackjack used her earned wages to pay for medical treatment for her son, Bennett.

---

### 2. Chronological Story Arc & Scene Beats (~60s)
- **Beat 1 (Verified Predicament)**: In September 1921, four men and twenty-three-year-old Ada Blackjack landed on uninhabited Wrangel Island in the Arctic Circle with only six months of rations.
- **Beat 2 (Constrained Choices)**: When the 1922 relief ship failed to break through the pack ice, supplies vanished, forcing three desperate crew members to attempt a frozen ocean trek to Siberia in January 1923—leaving Ada behind to nurse a bedridden, scurvy-stricken Lorne Knight.
- **Beat 3 (Documented Attempts & Setbacks)**: After Knight died in June 1923, Ada found herself entirely alone on the arctic rock with the expedition cat, facing brutal cold, meager game, and constant polar bear threats.
- **Beat 4 (Decisive Action & Verified Outcome)**: Mastering firearms, fox-trapping, and shelter maintenance entirely on her own, she sustained her life for two harrowing years until the relief ship *Donaldson* finally anchored in August 1923.
- **Beat 5 (Varied Engagement Close)**: Which survival skill mattered most during her isolation? Leave your choice below, and like and subscribe for more Against the Odds stories.

---

### 3. Visual & World-Building Canon
- **Setting & Era**: 1921–1923 Arctic Circle; stark, wind-scoured tundra, freezing ice-choked sea, desolate gravel beaches, primitive canvas tents, and rough wooden driftwood shelters.
- **Lighting & Mood**: Cold, oppressive arctic twilight, heavy shifting fog, pale low-angle sun glinting off jagged ice floes, and dark, moody contrasting shadows reflecting isolation and peril.
- **Wardrobe**: Heavy fur-trimmed parkas, weathered canvas expedition gear, thick mittens, and knit caps.
- **Character Appearance Consistency**: 
  - Protagonist: A minimalist clean black stick figure silhouette (solid black circle head, clean slender black stick limbs, zero facial features) wearing a thick, bulky insulated expedition down parka and hood [Template rule].
  - Accompanying entity: A tiny minimalist black cat silhouette representing Vic.
- **Mandatory 50/50 Media Split**: Alternating precise sequence of static concept art images and continuous motion concept art videos.

---

### 4. Scriptwriter Directives
- **Supported Hook**: Grounded strictly on the historical arrival date, crew composition, location, and initial 6-month ration constraint [Opening hook canon].
- **Next Factual Development**: Immediately introduce the failed resupply and the departure/disappearance of the three men attempting the ice trek, focusing the narrative on Ada's left-behind reality with Knight.
- **Key Constraints**: Financial desperation driving her to join, lack of prior Arctic training, absolute absence of outside communication, and severe physical isolation.
- **Decisive Contribution**: Self-taught hunting, trapping, nursing care, and unwavering determination to reunite with her hospitalized son.
- **Complete Outcome**: Knight and the three trekking men perished; Ada Blackjack and the cat survived and were rescued in August 1923. 
- **Faceless Depiction & Reconstruction Rules**: Adhere strictly to stickman silhouette framing with zero real human facial features or photorealistic rendering.
- **Engagement Close**: Ask a single case-specific question regarding her survival skills/decisions, coupled with standard like and subscription prompts within the target timeframe.

researchSources.snippet: A castaway is a person who is cast adrift or ashore. While the situation usually happens after a shipwreck, some people voluntarily stay behind on a desert island, either to evade captors or the world in general. A person may also be left ashore as punishment, known as marooning. The provisions and resources available to castaways may allow them to live on the island until other people arrive to take them off the island. However, such rescue missions may never happen if the person is not known to still be alive, if the fact that they are missing is unknown, or if the island is not mapped. These scenarios have given rise to the plots of numerous stories in the form of novels and film.
